title: Every whisper reaches Him, even the ones you cannot say
subtitle: As-Sami': the One who hears every voice, every language, every unspoken plea
intro: As-Sami' (السَّمِيعُ) means the All-Hearing: the One who hears every sound in creation, loud or silent, in every language at once, without one voice distracting Him from another. It means you are never talking to an empty room, and no prayer you make, however quiet or clumsy, goes unheard.

root.sense: Sam' is hearing, and it also carries the sense of listening with attention and accepting what is said, as in sami'na wa ata'na, we hear and we obey. As-Sami' is the intensive form: hearing that is complete, constant and attentive, and that answers.

row.title: He heard me before I finished
sub: and He was waiting for me to speak

knowing: As-Sami' hears everything that can be heard: a cry in a hospital ward, a footstep in the desert, the praise of birds, a sigh you did not mean to let out. He hears the open word and the private whisper equally. {idea}Billions call on Him at the same moment, in every language, and not one voice is lost or confused with another.{/idea} Human hearing tires, fades and mishears. His hearing never does.

His hearing is not only perception. It also means acceptance and response. When you say in prayer sami'a Allahu li man hamidah, Allah hears the one who praises Him, it means He hears with care and responds. So As-Sami' stands right beside Al-Mujib, the Responder. Like all His attributes, His hearing is real and perfect, and nothing in creation resembles it (42:11).

Why does the Quran so often put As-Sami' before Al-Basir and Al-Alim? Scholars of the Arabic language note that to hear someone you must be close to them. You can see someone from across a room and know a fact from a report years later, but hearing implies nearness. {idea}Placing hearing first is a reminder of how close He is to those who call Him.{/idea}
seeing: A woman named Khawlah came to the Prophet ﷺ to complain about how her husband had treated her. She spoke quietly in a corner of the room. Aisha, sitting nearby, later said she could not catch all of it, yet Allah revealed from above the heavens that He had heard the woman who argued about her husband and complained to Him (58:1). This is recorded by Imam Ahmad, an-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah. A private complaint about a private marriage became a verse recited until the end of time.

Ibrahim and Ismail, laying stones for the Kaaba, asked Allah to accept it and called Him the Hearing, the Knowing (2:127). The mother of Maryam, dedicating her unborn child, used the same words (3:35). When Musa and Harun were afraid to face Pharaoh, Allah said: Fear not, I am with you both; I hear and I see (20:46). Each time, His hearing is what gives a frightened or hopeful person the courage to act.
trusting: Most of us carry things we have never said out loud. We do not tell our parents because they will worry, our friends because they will judge, our spouse because the moment is never right. {reward}As-Sami' is the one place where you can say all of it.{/reward} He does not interrupt, get bored or say it is too late to call. He hears the prayer you cry in the car and the one you cannot even put into words.

His hearing also guards your tongue gently. The joke at someone's expense, the complaint about your parents, the half-true story, He heard those too. {trap}Speaking as if words disappear once they leave your mouth{/trap} is how small harms pile up. Knowing He hears makes you choose words you would be glad for Him to hear.
And when people plot or slander, you do not need to shout louder. He heard what was said in the room you were not in. Leave it with Him and keep your own words clean.
loving: Think of the person who listens to you best, who puts their phone down and really hears you. Now imagine Someone who always does that, for every one of His servants, at every moment, and who wants you to talk to Him. {idea}He did not just allow us to call Him; He asked us to.{/idea}
It is a lonely thing to call and get voicemail. With As-Sami' there is never voicemail, never a busy tone, never a queue. The heart warms to a Lord who is that attentive.
now: You are sitting in the car outside work, too tired to go in and too proud to tell anyone why. You do not even know how to put it into words. {idea}You do not need to. As-Sami' heard the sigh before the sentence.{/idea} Say whatever comes, in whatever language, and know it landed.
old: If I cannot find the right words, there is no point saying anything.
new: As-Sami' hears the broken sentence and the silent sigh, so I can speak to Him as I am.
try: Find two quiet minutes today and tell Allah, out loud and in your own words, one thing you have never told anyone.

dua.text: Ya Sami', You hear what I say and what I cannot say. Hear my call, accept my prayer, and let my tongue speak only what pleases You.
dua.note: Call on Him by this name whenever you begin a request or a good work, as Ibrahim and Ismail did at the Kaaba: Our Lord, accept from us, You are the Hearing, the Knowing (2:127).

pairs.why: As-Sami' hears every word and Al-Basir sees every movement; together they mean nothing about you is outside His attention (20:46).
As-Sami' hears your call and Al-Mujib answers it; hearing that leads to response is what makes prayer alive.
He hears your words and knows your whole situation, so even a poorly phrased prayer is understood fully.

faq.a: As-Sami' means the All-Hearing. Allah hears every sound and voice, secret or open, in every language at the same time, without one distracting Him from another. His hearing also implies that He accepts and responds to those who call on Him.

faq.q: Why does As-Sami' usually come before Al-Basir in the Quran?
faq.a: Some scholars of Arabic rhetoric explain that hearing someone requires being close to them, while seeing and knowing can happen from a distance. Mentioning hearing first emphasises how near Allah is to His servants. Whatever the reason, both are perfect attributes affirmed as befits Him.

faq.q: Which verse was revealed about a woman whose quiet complaint Allah heard?
faq.a: Surah al-Mujadilah begins with it (58:1). Khawlah bint Tha'labah complained to the Prophet ﷺ about her husband in a low voice. Aisha said she could not hear all of it, yet Allah revealed that He had heard her. The report is recorded by Imam Ahmad, an-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah.
